1127-othello:
Othello, a Moorish general in Venice's service, marries Desdemona in secret, and his ensign Iago, passed over for promotion, plots his ruin with lies about Desdemona and the young Cassio. William Shakespeare's tragedy follows Othello from love and trust to jealous rage and murder in Cyprus.

Iago, the most coldly brilliant villain in Shakespeare, works by hints and half-truths, and Othello's fall still shocks. Desdemona's innocence and Emilia's late courage frame the horror. The tragedy stands as a study of jealousy, race, and trust destroyed, and it grips every audience.
11680-george-eliot-a-critical-study-of-h:
George Willis Cooke's 1884 critical study takes up George Eliot's life, writings, and philosophy together. A preface to the second edition corrects an essay on lady novelists, first credited to Eliot, now known as George Henry Lewes's work, though its opinions match Eliot's own.

Chapters cover early life, work as translator and editor, and marriage, with later pages on Lewes's books on Spanish drama and Goethe. A passage on home scenes, with oaks, star-flowers, and speedwell, shows Cooke's claim that familiar fields are the mother tongue of imagination. The study is a Victorian appraisal, not a life alone.
12631-the-seven-little-sisters-who-live-:
Jane Andrews's Seven Little Sisters Who Live on the Round Ball That Floats in the Air, introduced by Louisa Parsons Hopkins, tells geography through seven girls around the world. A memorial of Andrews, born 1833 and died 1887, opens the book, followed by the ball itself, the little brown baby, Agoonack the Esquimau sister and how she lives through long summer.

Gemila, child of the desert, a little mountain maiden, Pen-Se, a little dark girl, Louise of the Rhine and Louise of the western forest complete the sisters. Andrews writes for three little friends, Marnie, Bell and Geordie, in simple, affectionate prose. The book is a classic children's geography, teaching the earth through imagined sisters.
12641-the-queen-of-the-air-being-a-study:
John Ruskin's Queen of the Air, a study of Greek myths of cloud and storm, grows from a lecture given partly at University College, London, on 9 March 1869. Athena Chalinitis, Athena in the heavens and Athena the Restrainer, who helped Bellerophon bridle Pegasus the flying cloud, fronts the book.

Ruskin asks permission to approach mythology in a temper unlike common treatment. He admits that we, like the Greeks, may err in faith, and that others' convictions, however singular, may hold truth where our own, however reasonable, may fail. Cloud, storm, Athena and nature symbolism follow. The book offers Ruskin at his most poetic and moral, reading myth as natural theology.
12819-dick-prescott-s-second-year-at-wes:
Dick Prescott's second year at West Point brings hazing lectures, Flirtation Walk, and a court-martial that tests his friends. Greg Holmes debates girls and mischief, while Cadet Dodge hears things he should not, and a false charge puts Dick under close arrest. A fight in the barracks and a riding drill discovery turn the tide.

Through it all Dick learns the soldier's glory is not parade shine but standing true when accused. Summer camp, visitors from home, and pitching for the Army nine lighten the strain. Hancock's tale mixes academy detail with a clean story of loyalty and honour.
13237-strange-visitors-a-series-of-origi:
Published in 1871, Strange Visitors claims to give papers by spirits of Irving, Willis, Thackeray, Brontë, Richter, Byron, Humboldt, Hawthorne, Wesley, and Browning, dictated through a clairvoyant in trance. Contents run from Margaret Fuller on literature in spirit life to Byron to his accusers, Hawthorne on apparitions, and Poe on the lost soul. The book is a spiritualist curiosity of its age.

One paper says Napoleon fell when he tore the magnetic filaments binding him to Josephine, like a wreck on St. Helena's shore. Another holds that each planet has a spirit world, with magnetic rays exchanging thoughts between earth and spirit globe. The papers mix philosophy, satire, and prophecy, and they show how Victorian readers sought voices from beyond.
1362-tom-swift-and-his-undersea-search-o:
Victor Appleton sends Tom Swift beneath the waves in a submarine of his own design, hunting a sunken treasure on the floor of the Atlantic. The tale moves through deep-sea wonders, rival salvors, and a wreck that guards its gold with storms and sharks.

Tom's inventions and his pluck carry the adventure, with his friends at his side. The book mixes science fiction with treasure-hunt thrills. It suits young readers who like Swift's formula of brains, machines, and danger under the sea. Swift's undersea hunt mixes science fiction with treasure thrills.
15602-statistical-historical-and-politic:
William Charles Wentworth, a native of the colony, published this statistical, historical, and political description of New South Wales in London in 1819, with Whittaker. Its subtitle promises an enumeration of advantages these colonies offer for emigration. It claims their superiority in many respects over those possessed by the United States. Four parts and an appendix carry the argument.

Part one gives a statistical account of settlements in New Holland. It opens with New South Wales on the eastern coast. That colony was first found by the Dutch in 1616, lying between nine and thirty-nine degrees south. Later parts judge fifteen years of government, suggest changes in policy, and propose changes in the system of rule. Wentworth writes as a colonial advocate, eager to draw settlers and reform, and the book is a founding document of Australian self-description.
16909-the-halo:
Bettina von Hutten wrote this 1907 novel, issued by Dodd, Mead in New York with a frontispiece by B. Martin Justice and a dedication to a dear lost friend. A prologue opens on a dusty Norman road, where an old blind man plays a cracked fiddle under apple trees, grinning as it shrieks, with a yellow dog beside him. No other living thing is in sight.

Von Hutten builds a tale of love, loss, and a halo of grace around flawed folk, in the high romantic style of her day. The Norman road and its fiddler set a mood of sorrow and wonder. Readers who like old romantic novels will find strong feeling, vivid scenes, and a story that asks what light can survive in broken lives.
20067-zun-i-fetiches-second-annual-repor:
Zuñi Fetiches appeared in the second annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. It studies sacred objects used by the Zuñi people of the Southwest. The text explains how people may give a thing in nature a life like their own. A force in nature can seem to act like an animal or a person.

Such reports were early United States attempts to record Native belief with care. The study names forms, uses, and beliefs tied to each fetish. Readers get a close, dated record of Zuñi faith as outsiders then saw it. It still serves those who study how such records were made.
20419-gigolo:
Gigolo tells a story of city nightlife, where dancers and hangers-on drift through clubs and dance halls. One woman keeps coming back despite repeated rebuffs. She leaves her name at the desk, hoping for word of the elusive Nick.

Smitty, Mike, or Elmer might bandy her name about, but she seems to lack the pride to stay away. The tale watches her hope against the cold rules of that world. It gives a sharp, unsentimental picture of the dance-hall scene and the people who lived for its lights and music.
2058-messer-marco-polo:
Brian Oswald Donn-Byrne, known as Donn Byrne, retells the life of Marco Polo as a romance. It follows the Venetian merchant from his youth to the court of Kublai Khan and his long road home. The author note stresses Byrne's Irish feeling. Donn-Byrne, born in New York and raised in Ireland, brought a Celtic lilt to his tales.

Byrne writes in a lyrical, old-world style, full of colour and adventure, and the book suits readers who like their history told as story. Marco's travels, wonders, and return give the novel its shape and its charm. His Marco Polo blends history with romance, so the traveller's marvels read like a storyteller's art.
20611-mr-grex-of-monte-carlo:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's Mr. Grex of Monte Carlo is a thriller of intrigue on the Riviera. Its hero looks in on a scene of casino splendor. After the first few moments of careless interest, his eyes undergo a curious change at what he sees.

He is contemplating one of the sights of the world: the gaming rooms of Monte Carlo in full blaze. Behind that glitter, the plot runs on spies, stolen plans, and disguised identities. Oppenheim wrote dozens of such tales, and this one shows his formula at its smoothest: bright rooms, dark purposes, and a gentleman in danger.
2267-othello:
Othello, a Moorish general in Venetian service, marries Desdemona in secret, and his ensign Iago sets out to destroy him. Othello moves from Cyprus's wars to a bedroom murder, as Iago plants a handkerchief and whispers doubts until jealousy unhinges a noble mind. Shakespeare makes the villain his most candid character, confiding his plans straight to the audience.

Desdemona's innocence and Emilia's late truth-telling sharpen the horror of the close. The play probes race, trust, and the ease with which love curdles into suspicion. It stands as one of the most painful tragedies ever staged.
23451-little-yellow-wang-lo:
M. C. Bell wrote this Dumpy Book for Children, number twenty six in the series, about Little Yellow Wang Lo, a boy who lives on a houseboat and tends ducks. Each morning he rises early, calls the ducks round the boat, feeds them, and watches them swim down river for fishes and frogs until supper time.

One hot day, Fo Pa, a very fat little man, sends him ashore in his Sunday clothes to sell the ducks at market and buy a pig for roasting. Wang Lo's eyes shine at the trip and at the thought of roast pork, and he rows off in haste, selling all his fat ducks in one market corner. The tale, with bright pictures, gives small children a warm glimpse of river life, work, and a boy's proud errand.
23889-charley-de-milo:
Larry M. Harris wrote Charley de Milo, a science fiction story set amid a carnival midway. Rockets climb, and Professor Lightning seems not to care. Outside talkers bark for grind shows, rides, and spectacles. Hell Drivers, the biggest auto show in fifty states, and dances learned at the court of the Sultan all cost the fourth part of a dollar bill.

The story's teasing premise is stated up front: a man might actually be held back by possessing two sound, working arms. With Hamlet's To be, or not to be as epigraph, Harris builds a midway tale around that odd idea. Kewpie dolls, Hawaiian leis, and a life-size model of Luna in three dimensions fill the midway.
28022-el-diablo:
Brayton Norton wrote El Diablo, illustrated by Dan Sayre Groesbeck and published in Indianapolis by Bobbs-Merrill in 1921, after copyright by Sunset Magazine. The novel opens with Richard Gregory waking fully dressed in thick grey fog, taking his automatic and rifle as a hand touches his shoulder.

Thirty-two chapters follow forbidden waters, jetsam, tangled threads, salvage, a strike, a battle at Northwest Harbor, and a fight in a cave, with the island's prisoner and the fangs of Mascola. Norton writes sea adventure with mystery and romance, in the popular magazine manner of the 1920s.
29557-the-lord-of-glory-meditations-on-t:
A. C. Gaebelein gathered these meditations on the person, work, and glory of Jesus Christ from the first pages of Our Hope magazine, where brief meditations had run for years. Copyrighted in 1910, the book was printed by the magazine's publication office in New York, with Pickering and Inglis of Glasgow and Toronto. Friends had urged that the notes be issued in book form so blessed truths might be preserved more permanently.

Gaebelein gives three reasons for the series. Christ is worthy of all honor and the first place in all things. His people need his person, past and present work, power, glory, and future manifestation kept before them. The meditations are short, devout, and plain. Readers of devotional literature will find a warm, earnest companion for daily reading.
30494-the-adventures-of-a-brownie-as-tol:
Miss Mulock tells The Adventures of a Brownie as told to her child, illustrated and copyrighted in 1908 by McLoughlin Brothers of New York. Six adventures follow Brownie with the cook, with the cherry tree, in the farmyard, on a ride, on the ice, and with the clothes.

Poems follow, including The Blackbird and the Rooks, The Shaking of the Pear-Tree, The Wonderful Apple-Tree, The Jealous Boy, The Story of the Birkenhead, Birds in the Snow, and The Little Comforter. Later verses add Don't Be Afraid, Girl and Boy, Agnes at Prayer, Going to Work, and Three Companions. Mulock blends fairy mischief with gentle verse for young children.
31273-the-arawack-language-of-guiana-in-:
D. G. Brinton's 1871 study, printed in Philadelphia, examines the Arawack language of Guiana in its linguistic and ethnological relations. The Arawacks, about two thousand souls living in British and Dutch Guiana between the Corentyn and Pomeroon rivers, call themselves lukkunu, men. Neighbors apply the contemptuous aruac, meal-eaters, for their diet of Mauritia palm pith and cassava root.

Brinton argues they once occupied the whole West Indian archipelago nearly to the northern continent. Whether their affiliations lie with northern or southern mainland tribes decides the course of primitive migration in the western world. He links them to the people Columbus and Peter Martyr described. The book is a foundational work of South American linguistics and ethnology.
32290-a-letter-to-a-gentleman-in-the-cou:
A Letter to a Gentleman in the Country, from His Friend in London, printed for and sold by J. Lacy in London in 1757 at one shilling, gives an authentic and circumstantial account of Admiral Byng. It covers his confinement, behaviour, and death, as attested by the gentlemen who were present. Its motto, Mens conscia Recti, a mind conscious of right, frames the account. The letter form promises an insider's report, not a historian's summary.

Lacy advertises companion pamphlets on the same case. They include Further Particulars from original papers by a gentleman of Oxford, and a collection of suppressed letters and detached pieces. A further address offers genuine copies of letters between Byng and the Secretary of the Admiralty. Readers get a contemporary pamphlet on one of the century's most debated executions, told by witnesses and sold while the controversy was fresh.
32762-michelangelo:
Romain Rolland tells the life of Michelangelo, translated by Frederick Street and published by Duffield and Company in 1921. Born at Caprese on March 6, 1475, Michelangelo grew from childhood and youth into the sculptor and painter of the Sistine ceiling, the David, the Pieta, and the tomb of Julius II.

Six chapters follow his work under Julius II, the failure of his great plans, his friendship with Vittoria Colonna, and his old age and death in 1564. Rolland closes by judging his genius and his grip on Italian art, arguing that later masters reflected their century while Michelangelo towered over it. Illustrations and a catalogue of works complete the volume.
4694-mademoiselle-of-monte-carlo:
William Le Queux published Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo in 1921, opening at a roulette table in Monte Carlo. A tall, good-looking young Englishman whispers to an older friend that the handsome woman winning at the table is the same woman he knows. He fears she might recognise him, and he longs to make her disclose what she knows about his poor father's mysterious end.

His friend doubts she ever will, given what is said about the Mademoiselle of Monte Carlo. From that first chapter, called The Suicide's Chair, Le Queux builds a thriller of gambling, secrets, and revenge on the Riviera. Readers get a fast, melodramatic mystery, with casinos, disguises, and a father's death to avenge, in the popular style of its day.
4924-dry-farming-a-system-of-agriculture:
Dry farming, as this manual explains it, means growing useful crops without irrigation on land receiving twenty inches of rain a year or less. In districts of torrential rain, high wind, or badly timed rainfall, the same methods apply up to twenty-five or even thirty inches, since water is lost faster than it falls.

The book sets out how to keep moisture in the soil, choose crops suited to dry country, and farm profitably where irrigation cannot reach. No author appears in the catalog record, but the system is laid out plainly for working farmers. Readers in arid regions get a practical guide to an agriculture built around saving every drop of rain.
britannica-1911-abati-niccolo: Niccolo Abati, also written Dell' Abbato, is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a famed fresco painter of Modena, with dates 1512 to 1571. His best works stand at Modena and Bologna, it states. He went with Primaticcio to France and helped deck the palace at Fontainebleau across two decades. Skill in drawing, grace, and natural color mark his pictures, the entry holds. One oil at Dresden, the martyrdom of St Peter and St Paul, ranks among his finest easel pieces.
britannica-1911-accorso-accursius-marian:
Mariangelo Accorso (about 1490-1544) was an Italian critic born at Aquila in the kingdom of Naples. A great favourite of the emperor Charles V, he spent thirty-three years at that court and travelled on foreign missions. To perfect Greek and Latin he added several modern languages, and his travels gave him rare chances to discover and collate, or compare, ancient manuscripts.

Scholarship of that kind fills his record. His Diatribae on Ausonius, Solinus, and Ovid is called a monument of learning and critical skill. He first edited the Letters of Cassiodorus, and his edition of Ammianus Marcellinus added five books beyond any earlier one. Accused of plagiarism in his notes, he repudiated the charge with great energy.
britannica-1911-agostino-paolo:
Paolo Agostino (1593-1629) was an Italian musician. He was born at Valerano. Giovanni Battista Nanini was his teacher in music. Dedications in his mass books record that debt. He later became his master's son-in-law. Agostino succeeded Ugolini as conductor of the pope's orchestra. That orchestra served in St Peter's at Rome. The post was among Italy's most prestigious musical offices.

Compositions are his claim on memory. His works are numerous, the entry says. Great merit is claimed for them collectively. One piece receives special admiration by name. It is an Agnus Dei written for eight voices. Eight-part writing showed a master's command of counterpoint. Brief as the entry is, it fixes his posts. Rome's papal chapel defined his career wholly.
britannica-1911-almelo:
Almelo is a town in the province of Overysel, Holland. It lies north-west of Hengelo at the junction of two canals. The Overysel and Almelo canals meet there. Its population in 1900 was 9,957. The place is of considerable antiquity. It was the seat of an independent lordship before the fourteenth century. Real importance came only in the second half of the nineteenth century.

That rise came from Almelo's share in the industrial growth of the Twente district. The town possesses numerous cotton and damask factories. Public buildings include a town hall and a court house. There is also a corn exchange. Churches of various kinds and a synagogue stand there. The entry traces the lordship's owners as well. The lords of Heeckeren gained Rechteren by marriage in 1350. They gained a countship in 1711. Their line remains established at Almelo.
britannica-1911-baccio-d-agnolo:
Baccio d'Agnolo (c. 1460-1543) was a Florentine wood-carver, sculptor, and architect, born Bartolommeo Baglioni and known by his shortened name, son of Angelo. He began in wood, carving much decoration for Santa Maria Novella and the Palazzo Vecchio between 1491 and 1502.

With his name made as a sculptor, Baccio turned to architecture. He helped restore the Palazzo Vecchio. In 1506 he was set to finish the drum of Florence cathedral's dome. Michelangelo's criticism stopped that work. He planned the Villa Borghese and the Bartolini palace, first house given columned fronts to doors and windows, a church-like novelty Florentines mocked. His studio drew Michelangelo, Sansovino, the Sangallo brothers, and the young Raphael.
britannica-1911-bartoli-daniello:
Daniello Bartoli (1608–1685), an Italian Jesuit priest born at Ferrara, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1623. Barred from the foreign mission field he had wanted, he won high standing instead as a preacher. He also taught rhetoric, the art of public speaking and writing, in Genoa, Florence, and Rome. Those cities, rather than distant missions, became the scene of his life's work.

Books carry Bartoli's reputation in the entry. Writing in Italian, he produced The Learned Man as an answer to the wide reading of romances. His larger work was a history of his order in six volumes, published at Rome from 1650 to 1673. The entry calls it especially informative about the early work of the Jesuits in Asia. Bartoli died at Rome, and collected editions of his works later ran to twelve volumes at Turin and fifty at Florence.
britannica-1911-baylo:
Baylo was the title of the Venetian representative at Constantinople, the Ottoman capital. The word comes from Latin forms linked to bailiff, and in Italian it appears as balio. At first the baylo acted much like a consul-general for Venice there.

From the 1600s on, the post also carried the rank and duties of a top-class diplomatic agent. A quoted account by A. de Wicquefort says the baylo served as consul and judge too. He settled cases among his own people and among all merchants who traded in the Levant under the flag of St Mark.
britannica-1911-carballo:
Carballo is a town of north-western Spain. It stands in the province of Corunna, in Galicia. It lies on the right bank of the river Allones. The city of Corunna is 20 miles north-east of it. Its population in 1900 was 13,032. This very short 1911 Britannica entry gives the town's plain facts. It adds its one line of local business.

Carballo is the central market of its district. That district is a thriving agricultural one, the entry says. Farmers bring their produce to the town to trade. Across the river stands San Juan de Carballo. Hot sulphurous springs rise at that village. The springs are the entry's one further point of interest. The whole notice runs to three short sentences. It gives the market role and the springs, and nothing more.
britannica-1911-cignani-carlo:
Cignani, Carlo (1628–1719) was an Italian painter, born of a noble family at Bologna, where he studied under Battista Cairo and then under Francesco Albani. Albani's most famous disciple, he was yet deeply shaped by Correggio as well. His greatest work, the Assumption of the Virgin round a cupola at Forlì, took some twenty years. That fresco plainly follows Correggio's more renowned cupola at Parma, the entry says.

Elaborate finish and bold artifice in colour mark the disciple of Albani, but Cignani gave his work a more thoughtful character than either model. Amiable, modest and generous as a man, he refused honours from princes and lived and died an artist. Envy led some enemies to deface certain works of his. His school at Bologna followed him when he removed to Forlì, and his son and nephew also painted.
britannica-1911-citta-di-castello:
Città di Castello is a town and episcopal see of Umbria, Italy, in the province of Perugia, on the left bank of the Tiber at 945 feet. It lies 38 miles east of Arezzo by rail, and its town people numbered 6,096 in 1901, with 26,885 in the commune. Inscriptions show it occupies the site of ancient Tifernum Tiberinum, near which Pliny had a villa. No remains of that town exist above ground today.

Totila devastated the town, yet it recovered and appears as Castrum Felicitatis late in the 8th century, with a bishopric from the 7th. Emperor and Church held it in turn until the Vitelli took it in 1468, after whose line died out it returned to the Church. Walls of 1518 ring its rectangle, and fine Renaissance palaces of the Vitelli stand inside. Some of Raphael's earliest works were painted for its churches, but none remains there.
britannica-1911-colonna-giovanni-paolo:
Giovanni Paolo Colonna (about 1637–1695) was an Italian musician born and raised in Bologna. He learned from Filippuzzi at home, then from Abbatini and Benevoli in Rome. In Rome he served for a time as organist at Saint Apollinare. A dated poem of praise shows that he made his mark as a composer by 1659.

That same year he became organist at Saint Petronio in Bologna. On 1 November 1674 he rose to chapel-master there. He also led the Philharmonic Academy of Bologna as president. Most of his work serves the church. Psalm settings for three to eight voices stand beside masses and motets. He wrote one opera, Amilcare, and one oratorio. The emperor Leopold I kept a copy of each piece he wrote. Vienna thus holds more than 83 of his church works. His style is called dignified in the main.
britannica-1911-crivelli-carlo:
Carlo Crivelli was a Venetian painter born in the earlier part of the 1400s. The only firm dates are 1468 and 1493, the earliest and latest years signed on his pictures. Though born in Venice, he worked chiefly in the March of Ancona, in and near Ascoli. He is said to have studied under Jacobello del Fiore. From 1490 he added the word Miles to his signature, having been knighted by Ferdinand II of Naples.

Crivelli painted in tempera only and shows best in subject pictures of moderate size. He liked landscape backgrounds and set fruits and flowers, above all the peach, as hanging garlands in his scenes. The entry calls his style hard in form and stern in feature, yet warm and distinct in colour. His Annunciation and Beato Ferretti hang in the National Gallery in London. Other named works sit at Berlin, in the Vatican, and in the Brera at Milan.
britannica-1911-dandolo:
Dandolo is the name of one of the great patrician families of Venice, first recorded among the electors of the first doge in 697. The family gave Venice four doges. The first and most famous was Enrico Dandolo, elected on 1 January 1193. Over seventy and of very weak sight, he still proved an energetic and able ruler. His first care was to restore Venetian power over the Dalmatians, though Zara held out against him.

In 1201 crusaders asked Venice for ships to carry 4,500 horse and 29,000 foot to Palestine, at 85,000 marks with half of all conquests. The crusaders could not pay, and Dandolo proposed that they first help him take Zara, with payment put off. The fleet of three hundred sail left on 8 October 1202 with the old doge in command.
britannica-1911-ermelo:
Ermelo is a district and a town of the Transvaal, and the entry treats both in a short notice. The district lies in the south-east of the province and is crossed by the Drakensberg. In it are Lake Chrissie, the only true lake in the country, and the sources of four rivers. The Vaal, Olifants, Komati, and Usuto all rise within 30 miles of one another there.

The region stands at a general height of about 5500 feet. It is fine farming and grazing country, and it also holds valuable minerals, including coal and gold. Ermelo town had 1451 people in 1904. It stands by rail 175 miles south-east of Johannesburg and 74 miles south-south-west of Machadodorp, on the Pretoria to Delagoa Bay line. A government experimental farm is kept at the town. That farm has some 1000 acres of plantations, the entry adds, closing a compact sketch of a high farming district.
britannica-1911-farini-luigi-carlo:
Luigi Carlo Farini (1812–1866), Italian statesman and historian, was born at Russi near Ravenna on 22 October 1812. A brilliant Bologna course broke off for the revolution of 1831. He then practised medicine at Russi and Ravenna and built a reputation. In 1843 his politics drew police suspicion, and he was expelled from the papal states. He lived in Florence and Paris, travelling as physician to Prince Jerome Bonaparte.

When Pius IX opened with liberal leanings, Farini returned as secretary-general to the interior minister in March 1848. He resigned on 29 April when the pope refused war on Austria. After the republic and the pope's return he withdrew to Turin. There he backed the House of Savoy in Cavour's press. His chief work, Lo Stato Romano dal 1815 al 1850, filled four volumes in 1850. He served as minister of public instruction in 1851–1852.
britannica-1911-fea-carlo:
Carlo Fea (1753-1836), Italian archaeologist, was born at Pigna in Piedmont on 2 February 1753 and studied law in Rome, taking his doctorate at the university of La Sapienza. Archaeology gradually took over his attention, and in 1798 he took orders to gain better chances for research. Driven to Florence for political reasons, he returned in 1799 and was jailed by the Neapolitans then holding Rome as a Jacobin.

Freed soon after, Fea became Commissario delle Antichita and librarian to Prince Chigi. He revised an Italian translation of Winckelmann's History of Art with notes, and annotated works by Bianconi. His own writings include a miscellany of philology and antiquities, a defence of the Pantheon's link to Agrippa, fragments of consular lists, inscriptions of public monuments, and a description of Rome. He died at Rome on 18 March 1836, having spent his later career among the city's antiquities.
britannica-1911-federici-camillo:
Camillo Federici (1749-1802), Italian dramatist and actor, was born at Garessio in Piedmont on 9 April 1749. His real name was Giovanni Battista Viassolo; Federici came from the title of an early piece, Camillo e Federico, and passed to his children. Educated at Turin, he loved literature and the theatre from youth. Praise for his first attempts fixed his career, and he worked with several companies as both writer and actor.

Federici married happily in 1777, left the stage, and settled at Padua to write. His many comedies spread his fame across Italy and for a time eclipsed his predecessors. Most are melodramatic, and he leaned on the moral tone found in Schiller, Iffland and Kotzebue. A merchant friend, Francis Barisan, kept him writing for a private theatre. Illness struck in 1791 and again as he prepared a collected edition. He died at Padua on 23 December 1802.
britannica-1911-folengo-teofilo:
Teofilo Folengo (1491-1544), known as Merlino Coccajo, was one of the chief Italian macaronic poets, mixing Latin with vernacular words for comic effect. He was born of noble parentage at Cipada near Mantua on 8 November 1491. From infancy he showed a lively mind and a rare cleverness at making verses. At sixteen he entered the monastery of Monte Casino near Brescia. Eighteen months later he became a professed Benedictine, and for a few years his monk's life ran regularly enough.

About 1516 Folengo left the cloister for the company of a well-born young woman, Girolama Dieda. They wandered the country for years, often in great poverty, living on his talent for verse. His first publication was the Macaronicon of Merlino Coccajo, the work that made his name. The entry follows his Latin verse and his macaronic poems, part mock-heroic and part satire.
britannica-1911-fresnillo:
Fresnillo is a town of the state of Zacatecas, Mexico, 37 miles north-west of the city of Zacatecas on a branch of the Santiago river. It held 6309 people in 1900 and stands about 7700 feet above the sea on a fertile plain between the Santa Cruz and Zacatecas ranges. The climate is temperate, and the farms around raise Indian corn and wheat.

The town's chief distinction is its school of mines, founded in 1853. Large amalgam works there treat silver ores from the mines of the neighbouring Proaño hill. Those mines were found in 1569 and for a time ranked among the richest in Mexico, but output fell sharply after the best deposits were reached in 1833. A station on the Mexican Central railway serves the town.
britannica-1911-godollo:
Godollo is a market town of Hungary, in the county of Pest-Pilis-Solt-Kiskun, 23 miles north-east of Budapest by rail. The 1911 Britannica entry gives it 5,875 people in 1900. It is the summer residence of the Hungarian royal family.

The royal castle was built in the second half of the 18th century by Prince Anton Grassalkovich. Castle and beautiful domain were presented by the Hungarian nation to King Francis Joseph I after the coronation of 1867. Stags and wild boars fill the park in great number. The entry calls the town a favourite summer resort for the people of Budapest. Nearby stands Maria-Besnyo, a famous place of pilgrimage with a fine Franciscan monastery holding the Grassalkovich family tombs.
britannica-1911-juarez-benito-pablo:
Benito Pablo Juárez (1806–1872), president of Mexico, was born near Ixtlan in the state of Oajaca on the 21st of March 1806, of full Indian blood. Left poor by his father's death, he gained schooling through a kind friar and then studied law. He began to practise in 1834 and rose fast as a voice for liberal views.

He governed Oajaca from 1847 to 1852, and was banished by Santa Anna in 1853. Back in 1855, he became minister of justice, then chief justice. When Comonfort was replaced in 1858, Juárez claimed the presidency by right of his office, and by 1861 had won it and been elected by congress. His halt on debt payments brought foreign troops to Mexico. France stayed, made war, and set Maximilian on a throne. Juárez held out in the north until Maximilian was taken and shot in 1867.
britannica-1911-la-tour-d-auvergne-theop:
Théophile Malo La Tour d'Auvergne (1743–1800), French soldier, was born at Carhaix in Brittany on the 23rd of December 1743, the son of an advocate named Corret. Set on a military career, he got himself enlisted in the Maison du Roi on a certificate of nobility signed by his friends. In 1771 he took the surname La Tour d'Auvergne, as a descendant of an illegitimate half-brother of Turenne.

Years of routine service were broken by volunteering with the Franco-Spanish expedition to Minorca in 1781, after which he refused promotion into the Spanish army rather than change allegiance. Made captain in 1784 and given the cross of St Louis in 1791, he opposed his brother officers' wish to emigrate rather than swear to the constitution. In 1792 he published a work on the Bretons. He won notice for courage in the Alps and harder fighting in the Pyrenees, yet declined promotion to colonel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-of-cas:
Adrian of Castello, also called de Corneto from his Tuscan birthplace, was an Italian prelate famed as statesman and learning's reviver, born about 1460, who died about 1521. Innocent VIII sent him as nuncio to Scotland in 1488, but recalled him on news of James III's death. Adrian had reached England and won Henry VII's favour, becoming his agent at Rome.

He went back to England as Peter's-pence collector in 1489, gained a St. Paul's prebend and a London rectory, and served in the papal treasury and as Henry's ambassador. Alexander VI made him cardinal in 1503, and he became Bishop of Hereford in 1502 and of Bath and Wells in 1504, though he never occupied the latter. Implicated in 1517 in a plot to poison Leo X, he confessed, was forgiven, fled to Venice, and was degraded from the cardinalate in 1518.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Oslo occupied part of the site of Christiania, founded in 1624. After Hamar was formed in 1152, Oslo was limited to Christiania, Smaalenene, Jarlsberg and Laurvik, and Akershus in Norway, with Goteborg and Bohus in Sweden. Rudolf, a court bishop brought by Saint Olave from Rouen, worked at Sarpsborg from 1015 to 1030, but Asgaut, from 1047 to 1072, is usually counted the first Bishop of Oslo.

Nicholas Arnesson, bishop from 1190 to 1225, played a great though unhappy part in Norwegian politics. Haakon, from 1248 to 1265, gave generously to his chapter before moving to Trondhjem. Solomon, from 1322 to 1352, was the only Norwegian bishop to survive the Black Death in 1349, and in 1350 he consecrated bishops for Bergen and Skalholt in Iceland. In 1352 Pope Clement VI made Gyrd Aslesson exchange sees with Sigfrid of Stavanger. Eystein, from 1385 to 1407, helped negotiate the union of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under Queen Margaret in 1397.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-and-p:
Antonio and Piero Benci Pollajuolo, Florentine brothers born in 1432 and 1443, took their name from their father's poultry trade. Antonio trained under Uccello and worked as painter, sculptor, and goldsmith, while Piero learned in his brother's studio. From 1465 they worked together, and both died at Rome and share one tomb in Saint Peter in Chains.

Antonio's own paintings include David and three labours of Hercules, small panels now at Berlin and the Uffizi. As a sculptor he cast the bronze tomb of Sixtus the Fourth in Saint Peter's, its portrait head crowned with the tiara. Piero painted altarpieces of his own, and the entry presents two brothers who joined craft, muscle, and devotion in Renaissance Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bartolome-est:
Bartolomé Esteban Murillo was a Spanish painter born at Seville in 1617, who died there in 1682. Esteban was his family name; Murillo, his mother's, he took by Andalusian custom. Orphaned at ten, he was raised by his barber uncle and studied under Juan del Castillo, a mediocre painter but good teacher. To live, he painted cheap sargas on rough canvas, sold at country fairs and shipped to America.

In Madrid, Velasquez, a fellow Sevillian, opened the royal galleries to him, where he studied Titian, Veronese, Tintoretto, and Rubens for three years. He returned to Seville in 1644 and left it only once more, for Cadiz in 1681, to paint a Capuchin altar he never finished. A fall from scaffolding or a serious illness ended that work, by differing accounts. His Immaculate Conceptions remain his most famed devotional works, genuinely religious in feeling.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedetto-mar:
Benedetto Marcello, a Venetian composer and public servant, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Venice in 1696 and dead at Brescia in 1739, he mixed politics with art throughout his life. He served as provveditore, a Venetian overseer, at Pola, then as camerlengo, a finance officer, at Brescia, where failing health ended his service.

Music, though, is his lasting claim. Manuscripts of his musical theory and his operas survive in Venice, Dresden, and Brussels. His best work, by the entry's judgment, is his paraphrase of the Psalms, a setting of the biblical songs in verse. The piece sketches a nobleman who governed by day and composed at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benvenuto-tis:
Benvenuto Tisio, called Garofalo after his birthplace, was a painter of the Ferrara school, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born in 1481, he died at Ferrara in 1559. With Mazzolino and Dosso Dossi he forms the modest trio of sixteenth-century Ferrarese painting, heir to an earlier school famed for the Schifanoja Palace frescoes.

Early promise showed in hunting and procession scenes painted with a romantic eye, learned under Panetti and Costa and coloured by Venetian lessons at Cremona. Three years in Rome then bent him toward Raphael and Michelangelo, a spell the entry judges costly to his own voice. His later work never quite regained its first freshness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernal-diaz-d:
Bernal Díaz del Castillo, a Spanish chronicler of the conquest of Mexico, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Medina del Campo about 1498, he died after 1568. A common soldier of poor parents, he sailed to America in 1514, reached Yucatán in 1517, and marched into Mexico with Cortés.

He claims a part in 119 battles and was present at the fall of Mexico City, a claim the entry treats as a soldier's honest record. His True History, written late in life, answers more polished accounts with an eyewitness voice. The piece presents the conquest as one foot soldier saw and remembered it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-agostino-n:
Blessed Agostino Novello, born Matteo di Termini in Sicily during the early thirteenth century, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His village belonged to Palermo's archdiocese, so he is sometimes called Panormitano. His noble Catalan family schooled him carefully in the sciences of his day.

On entering religion he took the name Agostino, with Novello added for his learning and virtue. He served as a high official of the Augustinian order, then retired to a hermitage at San Leonardo, where miracles were reported at his tomb. The entry presents a scholar turned hermit, honoured by two cities claiming him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-buffalo:
Buffalo, a diocese set up on 23 April 1847, covers eight New York counties across 6,357 square miles, nearly a third of the state. Cut from the great New York diocese with its see on Lake Erie, it lost its eastern counties to Rochester in 1868 and four more after Bishop Ryan's death in 1896. Before white settlers came, Senecas and Cayugas of the Iroquois League held the region.

Seneca raids carried Huron Christian captives from Canada into a village called Saint Michael's, visited by Jesuits in 1656. Fremin built a chapel there in the fall of 1668 and said the first Mass on 3 November 1668. Pierron followed at Gannagaro, or Saint James, in 1671, while Carheil raised Saint Joseph's chapel among the Cayugas in November 1668. Other chapels, like the Immaculate Conception at Totiakton near Lima, served four or five flourishing Jesuit missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capaccio-and-:
Capaccio and Vallo form a suffragan diocese of Salerno in southern Italy, with the bishop residing at Vallo. Capaccio stands near the ruins of ancient Paestum. It is thought to have been built after Saracens destroyed Paestum in 915, when the see moved there. Its first known bishop was Arnolfo, present at the Lateran council of 1179.

Later bishops named in the entry include the zealous monk Pietro Matta de Haro, Tommaso Caraffa, and Giovanni della Pace, along with the learned Cardinal Francesco Maria Brancacci. Lelio Morello moved the bishop's residence to Dania under Sixtus V. The diocese counted 122,400 people with 102 parishes, 282 churches and chapels, and hundreds of priests, plus three religious houses for men.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cignani-famil:
An entry on the Cignani, three Bolognese painters of one family, headed by Carlo, born in 1628. A count of noble birth, Carlo studied under Albani, felt the Carracci strongly, and followed Correggio. His first major work decorated Cardinal Farnese's great salon at Bologna, and his plague scenes in San Michele in Bosco, each upheld by two angels of remarkable beauty, show Correggio's manner. A palace interior for the Duke of Parma won him knighthood.

Carlo's masterpiece, the Assumption of the Virgin, fills the cupola of Forlì cathedral, painted from 1681 to 1706. After it he held high town office and presided over Bologna's academy under Clement the Eleventh. His colour is suave, his drawing largely accurate, and his facility extraordinary, though grandeur outruns execution. He died at Forlì in 1719. His son Felice, born 1660, painted for pleasure from a large fortune, and his nephew Paolo, born 1709, left only three known paintings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citta-di-cast:
Citta di Castello, in the province of Perugia in Umbria, stands on an Apennine slope near the Tiber, on the site of ancient Tifernum. Pliny built a splendid villa there. In 550 Fantalogus, acting for Totila, the Ostrogothic king, took and destroyed the city, later rebuilt around a castle, giving it its name. By Pepin's donation in 752 it came under the Holy See.

Later centuries saw Guelph and Ghibelline rule, a rising against the States of the Church in 1375, and capture by Braccio da Montone in 1420 under Martin the Fifth. Nicolo Vitelli ruled as tyrant until Sixtus the Fourth's siege in 1474 forced his surrender. The city also claims martyrs under Diocletian, its first-known bishop Ennodius in 465, and Pope Celestine the Second, born there. Its cathedral keeps a twelfth-century silver altar-front and a fifteenth-century crosier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-council-in-tr:
The Council in Trullo, a Constantinople synod of 692 under Justinian II, met in the domed hall that gave it its name. Called Quinisext, or Fifth-Sixth, it supplied the disciplinary canons the Fifth and Sixth General Councils had omitted. All 215 bishops in attendance were Eastern, and they issued 102 canons, largely reaffirming earlier ones.

Western churches never recognised those canons, which renewed old decrees, condemned the heresy of Honorius, and pressed Constantinople's customs on the whole Church. Celibacy rules drew the sharpest line: clerics below bishop might remain married, and none might separate a priest from his wife. Eastern Orthodoxy still counts the council ecumenical.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-enrico-dandol:
Enrico Dandolo was Doge of Venice from 1192 to 1205, dying at a hundred years old. He came from an electoral family descended from the twelve tribunes who chose the first doge in 697. A kinsman was Patriarch of Grado for fifty years. A man of uncommon physical and mental strength, he took the cross at nearly a hundred and led the expedition against Constantinople. He was a fearless knight and a diplomat, predominant in the Fourth Crusade.

He first appears in the war with Emperor Manuel Comnenus in 1171, when plague-struck Venetians lay at Chios and Dandolo was sent to Constantinople for peace. Tradition says the emperor burned out his eyes, though later writers hold he was partly blinded. Elected doge on 1 June 1192, he settled quarrels with Verona. He warred on Zara and the Pisans. He made a treaty with Emperor Alexis III in 1198, before Venice fell out with Alexis in 1201.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernest-hello:
Ernest Hello, a French philosopher and essayist, was born at Lorient in Brittany on 4 November 1828 and died at Kéroman, near Lorient, on 14 July 1885. Delicate health dogged him from infancy, and it hampered his work badly while giving his writings their melancholy tone.

At school in Rennes, and later at the College Louis-le-Grand in Paris, he stood first in his classes. He graduated at fifteen. His father's wishes sent him to law, and brilliant examinations won his admission. Yet he refused the profession, because his comrades had decided that a lawyer could not in conscience defend an unjust cause. Admiration for Gratry and Lacordaire drew him toward theology. Abbé Baudry, afterwards Bishop and then a professor at Saint-Sulpice, instructed him in it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-estevan-cabri:
Estevan Cabrillo was a Portuguese in Spain's naval service, born at an unknown date and place, dead on San Bernardo on 3 January 1543. In 1541 Pedro de Alvarado gathered twelve vessels at Navidad, on Western Mexico's coast, for an expedition to the Moluccas. Alvarado was soon killed assaulting the rock of Nochiztlan, defended by hostile Indians. The Viceroy Mendoza sent most of the squadron under Villalobos to the Moluccas, and two large vessels north under Cabrillo.

Cabrillo sailed from Navidad in 1542, coasting slowly upwards owing to contrary winds. In his voyage he discovered Santa Catalina, the Santa Barbara channel, Monterey, Cape Mendocino, and the Oregon coast to latitude 43 degrees. Scurvy broke out violently, so he could make only a short stay on Oregon and Northern California shores, and had to turn back. His treatment of the aborigines was particularly kind and generous.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-faustino-arev:
Faustino Arevalo was a learned Spanish Jesuit who wrote hymns and studied the early Fathers. Born in 1747, he joined the Society in 1761 and was sent to Italy. Lorenzana, his patron, paid for his books and put him in charge of them. Arevalo later served the pope as hymn writer, theologian, and adviser in Rome.

His Hymnodia Hispanica of 1786 gave old Spanish hymns back their true metrical form. He also put out new texts of Prudentius, Dracontius, Juvencus, and Sedulius. Called back to Spain in 1815, he led the Castille province from 1820. Arevalo died at Madrid in 1824, famed for deep and scholarly learning and love of Spain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gasparo-molo:
Gasparo Molo, an Italian goldsmith and medalist of the seventeenth century, cut the dies of popes and princes. Born near Como or Lugano, he worked at Milan and Mantua, then at Florence from 1608 as master of the mint stamps. His medals for Cosimo II's marriage and accession in 1609 made his name, and he cut talers and merit medals for the grand duke.

About 1623 Molo moved to Rome as die-cutter at the papal mint, striking coins and medals under Urban VIII, Innocent X, and Alexander VII into 1664. A faithful portraitist and fine figure composer, he favored the stamped medal over the cast, and his stamped work ranks among the best of its age. His pupil Hamerani, founder of a long line of mint artists, carried his school forward.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Castello, called Il Bergamasco, was an Italian painter, sculptor, and architect born at Gandino in 1509, who died at Madrid in 1579. Left unprotected at Genoa as a young man, he won the protection of Tobia Pallavicino, who sent him to Rome to study the masters. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows him from Genoa palaces to the Spanish court.

Back in Genoa he decorated his protector's palace and painted the martyrdom of St. Sebastian. He worked with Luca Cambiaso in the Nunziata di Portoria. At Gorlago he painted scenes from the Iliad in the Lanzi Palace hall. Invited to Spain by Philip II in 1567, he adorned the Pardo with Ovidian subjects, worked at the Escorial, and died as architect of the royal palace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isleta-pueblo:
Two pueblos of the ancient Tigua people share the name Isleta, and this entry tells them apart. The older and chief town stands on the Rio Grande's west bank about twelve miles below Albuquerque, New Mexico. Its offshoot, Isleta del Sur, lies on the Texas side a few miles below El Paso. Spaniards named the first for its tongue of land jutting into the stream, while the native name Shiewhibak points to a knife used in a ceremonial foot race.

Coronado first entered Isleta in 1540, Espejo followed in 1582–83 seeking three murdered Franciscans, and before 1629 it housed the Franciscan mission of San Antonio. Later it sheltered refugees from outlying pueblos. The entry blends Spanish exploration, mission planting, and Tigua life into a short frontier history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jemez-pueblo:
Jemez Pueblo, an Indigenous town on the north bank of the Jemez River some twenty miles northwest of Bernalillo in New Mexico, shelters the last remnant of a people. They held some ten villages when Spaniards first met them in 1541. Neighbours named them Jemez; they call their town Walatoa, Bear Village.

Coronado entered their country in 1541, and Franciscans gathered them into two mission villages about 1618. After joining the great Pueblo rising of 1680, they were stormed by Vargas in 1694, fled to the Navajo after a 1696 revolt. They later returned to build their present pueblo. Smallpox in 1728 and 1780 cut them hard, leaving about five hundred souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-juan-de-dicas:
Juan de Dicastillo was a Spanish Jesuit theologian born at Naples in 1584 to Spanish parents. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1600 and taught theology for twenty-five years at Toledo, Murcia, and Vienna. In moral questions he followed the probabilists, who held that a probable opinion may be safely followed.

His chief works treat justice and the cardinal virtues, the sacraments in general, oaths and church censures, and the Incarnation, all published at Antwerp between 1641 and 1662. Dicastillo died at Ingolstadt in 1653. The entry lists his books as the solid output of a long teaching career rather than a single famous work.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludovicus-a-s:
Ludovicus a S. Carolo, also known as Ludovicus Jacob, was a French Carmelite writer and librarian, born at Chalons in 1608 and dead at Paris in 1670. Son of Jean Jacob, he joined the Old Observance Carmelites in his home town and professed in 1626.

In Italy in 1639 he fell in love with inscriptions, lamenting their wholesale ruin in the catacombs, and finished Naude's Bibliotheca Pontificia at Rome. Back in France he served Cardinal de Retz and President Harlay as librarian, and became royal councillor and almoner. He also launched the first yearly lists of printed books, Paris lists for 1643 to 1645, a trade his successors still follow.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luis-antonio-:
Luis Antonio Arguello was a governor of California, born at San Francisco in 1784 and dead there in 1830. His family ranked among the most influential in early California, and his father served as acting governor in 1814 and 1815, then governor of Lower California to 1822.

Luis succeeded his father as comandante in 1806, became captain in 1818, and governed from November 1822 to 1825. He was the only governor under the Mexican Empire and the first California native to hold the office. In 1821 he led the famed expedition to the Columbia, the widest Spanish exploration of the north country ever made from California, and left a name for honesty, ability, and kindness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marco-polo:
Marco Polo was a Venetian traveller, born in 1254 and dead there in 1324. His father Nicolo and uncle Matteo, sons of the patrician Andrea Polo, traded at Constantinople and Sudak in the Crimea. About 1255 they left Constantinople with jewels for Barka, Mongol Khan of Kipchak, who paid them well.

War with Hulagu of Persia stranded them, and they pushed east to Bokhara, staying three years. Envoys of Hulagu to the Great Khan carried them onward, and after three years' travel they reached Acre in 1269 with a Mongol baron. Marco soon won Kublai's affection, learning four Tatar tongues and scripts. Home again, the family looked and dressed like Tatars and had nearly lost their Venetian speech. Marco's Book, dictated to Rusticiano in French, tells the journeys, Kublai's realm, and the failed sea attack on Japan, surviving in eighty-five manuscripts with notable differences.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matteo-bandel:
Matteo Bandello was born at Castelnuovo di Scrivia in Piedmont in 1480 and died as Bishop of Agen, France, in 1565, though other sources give 1485 to 1561. He joined the Dominicans, but his life and writings show slight religious trace. He is best known by his Novelle, 214 tales in three volumes at Lyons in 1554, with a fourth in 1573.

These tales display real literary skill but do the churchman no credit, many being perverse accounts of horrors and wickedness. Many were translated into English by Painter and gave themes to Elizabethan dramatists. Most likely through that channel Shakespeare learned the Romeo and Juliet story. Byron later took up Bandello's Parisina tale. The best Novelle edition is Silvestri's Milan edition of 1813 to 1814 in nine volumes. Some tales appear in the Tesoro dei Novellieri Italiani of Paris, 1847, and some were translated by Roscoe in Italian Novelists of 1825.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mazzara-del-v:
Mazzara del Vallo, a diocese in the province of Trapani, Sicily, sits on the Mediterranean at the mouth of the Mazzara River. The town trades largely in lemons, boasts mineral springs nearby, and stands on the site of ancient Selinus's market port. A Megarian colony settled it in 630 B.C. Carthage took it in 409 B.C., and in 249 it was razed, its people deported to Lilybaeum.

A new town grew around the port, fell to the Saracens in 827, and became capital of one of their three Sicilian valli. Count Roger routed the Saracens there in 1075, and the see of Lilybaeum moved to Mazzara. Its bishops include Paschasinus, legate at Chalcedon, Stefano de Ferro, the first bishop in 1093, Cardinal Bessarion, and founders of cathedral, library, and seminary. The entry traces the see through conquest and rebuilding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-othlo:
Othlo, also spelled Otloh, was a Benedictine monk of Saint Emmeram's at Ratisbon, born in 1013 in the Diocese of Freising and dead in 1072. Schooled at Tegernsee and Hersfeld, Bishop Meginhard summoned him to Wuerzburg for his skill in writing. He entered the order in 1032, became dean in 1055, and took charge of the monastic school. To escape Bishop Otto's oppression he fled to Fulda in 1062, returning to Ratisbon in 1067.

Young Othlo loved the classics, above all Lucan, but later judged them unfit for religious minds and sought to replace pagan authors with his own edifying writings. Modest and pious, he opposed dialectics as bondage to set forms. He stands accused of starting the tale that Saint Denis the Areopagite's relics reached Ratisbon, and of forging exemption letters for his abbey. His Dialogue on his own trials marks the start of medieval autobiography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pedro-angulo:
Pedro Angulo, a native of Burgos in Spain, came to America in 1524 as a soldier. He joined the Dominicans in 1529 and became a companion of Las Casas in Guatemala, Central America generally, and the greater Antilles. Made Dominican provincial for Chiapas and Bishop of Vera Paz, he died soon after, in 1561. He ranks among the earliest Indian missions' chief figures in southern Mexico and Guatemala, judged to outstrip Las Casas in importance, ability, and success.

His devotion to the work overcame every obstacle: he went from tribe to tribe, living and teaching among them. Seeing Indians grasp things more by eye than ear, he used charts where Bible subjects were shown allegorically. He carried them through wilderness as illustrations for his talks to natives. He mastered two Indian tongues, Nahuatl and Zutuhil, and wrote several religious tracts in the latter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-fullo:
Peter Fullo was a usurping Monophysite patriarch of Antioch who died in 488. His Greek surname, Gnapheus, came from his trade as a fuller of cloth, worked while he was a monk among the Sleepless Monks near Chalcedon. Expelled for loose living and heretical teaching, he won a priest's post through the future emperor Zeno, then stirred Antioch against Patriarch Martyrius and seized the see in 470.

His badge was a phrase added to the Trisagion, saying the Crucified One suffered for us in a sense that made Father and Spirit share the cross. The emperor deposed him in 471, he seized the see again in 476, was banished in 478, and was restored by the usurper Basiliscus in 485. He held Antioch until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-capero:
Pietro Caperolo was a Franciscan preacher whose energy split a province of his order in the 1470s. He was a Friar Minor of unknown birth date, prized as a preacher at Brescia, Velletri, and other north Italian cities. He threw himself into the quarrel between the Franciscan provinces of Milan and Venice, sharpened by war between the two states.

With much effort he won Pope Sixtus IV's leave to detach several Venetian convents from the Observants. He formed a vicariate under the Conventuals that still chose its own superior. His followers were called Caperolani after him, but on his death at Velletri in 1480 the new branch dissolved, and every house returned to the Observants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pinerolo:
Pinerolo is a Piedmontese city and diocese in northern Italy, long a key fortress of the dukes of Savoy. It was first mentioned in the tenth century and ruled at first by its abbots. It passed under Savoyard protection in 1235 and full control in 1243, fell to France in 1536 and again in 1630, and returned to Savoy by the Treaty of Turin.

Its churches include a ninth-century cathedral with a fine bell tower and the Gothic San Maurizio, whose belfry looks out over the Alps. Founded as an abbey in 1064 by Adelaide of Susa and made a diocese in 1748, it counts fifty-eight parishes, and within its bounds stands the famous fortress of Fenestrelle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reyer-anslo:
Reyer Anslo, Dutch poet and convert, was born at Amsterdam in 1622 and died at Perugia in 1669. His parents were Mennonites, and he was baptized on 16 November 1646 and raised in that sect. Already famous as a poet, he earned his native city's laurel crown and silver dish for a poem honouring the new town hall. A poem honouring Sweden's Queen Christina, the Swedish Pallas, won him a golden chain.

In 1651 he entered the Catholic Church with forty-three others, as Jesuit manuscript records attest. In Rome he became secretary to Cardinal Capponi and received a gold medal from Pope Innocent the Tenth for his poetry. His works include a tragedy, The Parisian Blood-Bridal, on the Massacre of Saint Bartholomew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rodriguez-san:
Rodriguez Sanchez de Arevalo was a learned Spanish bishop and writer on church and state. Born in 1404 in the diocese of Segovia, he studied law at Salamanca for ten years and graduated as doctor. He served John II and Henry IV of Castile as secretary and envoy, opposing the Council of Basle's parliamentary theories at the Holy See.

After Calixtus III rose, he stayed at Rome and became Bishop of Oviedo. He later commanded the Castle of St Angelo under Paul II, who moved him in turn to Zamora, Calahorra, and Palencia. Printed works include the Speculum Vitae Humanae of 1468, on the lights and shadows of life's estates. They include the Historia Hispanica to 1469 and De Monarchia Orbis of 1521, asserting the pope's sole right to punish kings. His bold rebukes led Matthaeus Flaccus to call him a forerunner of Luther, quite unjustly, as Niccolo Antonio showed. He died in 1470.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saltillo:
Saltillo, a Mexican diocese suffragan of Linares, or Monterrey, covers the state of Coahuila, 63,728 square miles, with 357,652 people by the 1910 census. Its chief city, Saltillo, sits 5,190 feet above sea level and counted 35,063 people, serving as home to both bishop and state governor. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces a frontier see.

Founded in 1575 by Francisco de Urdinola, the city mixed Huachichil and Borrado Indians with Tlaxcalans brought by the Spanish, and Franciscan Andrés de León preached there in the sixteenth century. Renamed Ciudad Leona Vicario in 1827 for a Mexican heroine, it kept its old name in practice. Jalisco Franciscans held eight Coahuila missions under Linares until Leo XIII erected Saltillo as its own see in 1891.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-gallo:
San Gallo names a celebrated family of architects, sculptors, painters, and engravers who flourished in Renaissance Italy from the mid-fifteenth to the late sixteenth century. Founder Francesco Giamberti, a Florentine wood-carver who lived from 1405 to 1480, fathered Giuliano and Antonio. Their entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a dynasty of makers.

Giuliano da Sangallo, architect and sculptor from 1445 to 1516, trained under Francione, then went to Rome. Study of Vitruvius fired his love of antiquity there, and he worked on the Palace of San Marco for Cardinal Barbo, later Paul II. Back in Florence he shone as a military engineer, fortifying Ostia harbour in 1483 for Cardinal della Rovere, and spent his later years in Medici service and protection. The entry traces the family's buildings and fortunes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-francis-ca:
Francis Caracciolo, co-founder of the Minor Clerks Regular, found his vocation in a letter delivered to the wrong man. Baptized Ascanio in 1563 at Villa Santa Maria in the Abruzzi, he was cured of leprosy at twenty-two and vowed himself to church life, giving his goods to the poor. Studying theology at Naples, he was ordained in 1587 and joined the Bianchi della Giustizia, who helped condemned criminals die holy deaths. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Agnone to 4 June 1608.

A letter from Giovanni Agostino Adorno, seeking another Ascanio Caracciolo for a new institute, reached our saint by mistake in 1588. He read the error as God's will, helped draft the congregation's rules, and saw Sixtus V approve it on 1 July 1588. The entry turns a postal slip into a founding, and a leper's cure into a priest's career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gaspare-de:
Gaspare del Bufalo founded the Missionaries of the Most Precious Blood after a childhood cure he credited to Francis Xavier. Born at Rome on Epiphany 1786 to Antonio, chief cook of the Altieri princes, and Annunziata Quartieroni, he was confirmed at eighteen months for delicate health. An eye malady threatening blindness yielded to prayers to Xavier in 1787, and Gaspare kept the apostle as his congregation's patron. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 28 December 1837.

From childhood he showed horror even of venial sin, deep piety, mortification, mastery of a fierce temper and strong will, and heroic love for the poor. Entering the Collegium Romanum at twelve, he took first tonsure in 1800. The entry's early chapters show a Roman boy, frail of eye and strong of will, formed for a missionary order devoted to Christ's blood.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-odilo:
Odilo, fifth abbot of Cluny, turned a single great monastery into the centre of a reforming network. Born about 962 to Auvergne nobility, he entered Cluny in 991 and became abbot before Mayeul's death in 994. Gentleness, charity, and a talent for organisation drove rapid growth under his rule.

He encouraged learning, set Radolphus Glaber to write a history of the age, and raised a magnificent monastery church. Monasteries under Cluny grew from thirty-seven to sixty-five, with five newly founded and twenty-three reformed. His reform reached Spain under Alfonso VI and prepared the union of houses that Hugo later completed. He died on 31 December 1048, famed for prayer and for All Souls' Day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-teilo:
Teilo, archbishop of Llandaff, shaped the Welsh Church from a monastic school that bore his name. Born at Eccluis Gunniau near Tenby, cousin of David, he was educated by Dyfrig at Hentland and by Paulinus at Whitland. He later ruled the monastic school at Llandaff, called Bangor Deilo after him.

The earliest lives are late and uncritical. A tale of his visit to Palestine with David and Padarn about 518, with consecration by John III of Jerusalem, is not now generally credited. His true name may have been Eliau, appearing in Latin as Teliarus and in Breton as Teliau. He died at Llandilo Vawr, probably in or before 560, an old man, though Ussher puts his death at 604.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taos-pueblo:
Taos is an important Pueblo town on the Taos River in New Mexico. It lies about fifty miles northeast of Santa Fe. Its people speak Tigua, of Shoshonean stock. From some 2,500 people in 1630 and 2,000 before the revolt of 1680, it shrank to 578 in 1788. It stands now at about 450. Coronado's men first reached it in 1540. Franciscans founded San Geronimo de Taos about 1620.

In the great revolt of 1680, Taos served as headquarters of Pope, the rebellion's leader. Its two missionaries were killed. Missions revived after the reconquest some fifteen years later, then faded under Ute and Navaho raids. In 1847 townsfolk resisting American rule killed Governor Bent and others. American troops stormed the town, killing some 150 and executing sixteen more. The old feast of San Geronimo on 30 September still draws crowds for a relay race.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tiepolo:
Tiepolo covers two Venetian painters, father and son, in a single entry. Giovanni Battista Tiepolo was born at Venice in 1696, the son of a sea captain who left a good fortune. He married Cecilia Guardi in 1721 and fathered nine children. Studying Titian, Piazzetta, Ricci and above all Veronese, he became the last great Venetian painter.

He worked in Venice and northern Italy until 1750, spent three years painting ceilings at Wurzburg, and in 1761 went to Madrid at Charles III's invitation to decorate the royal palace. There the rivalry of Raphael Mengs embittered his last years, and he died at Madrid in 1770. His son Giovanni Domenico, born in 1727, assisted him but never matched his draughtsmanship or colour.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trujillo:
A diocese in north-west Peru, comprising Lambayeque, Libertad, Piura and the province of Tumbes. Gregory XIII formed it on 13 April 1577 as a suffragan of Lima. Its city was founded in 1535 by Gonzalo Pizarro on the Río Muchi and named for his native place. It became the first Peruvian city to proclaim independence from Spain.

Most houses stand only one story high because of frequent earthquakes, the worst in 1619, 1759 and 1816. Near the city lie the ruins of Gran Chimu, or ChanChan, stretching twelve miles by six, with walls nine metres high and great burial mounds. From these ruins the Spaniards recovered over £5,500,000 in gold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-uccello:
Paolo Uccello was a Florentine painter born in 1397 who died in 1475. He is famed less for his given name than for his nickname, earned from his love of painting birds. His real name was Paolo di Dono. Apprenticed to Ghiberti, he helped prepare the first bronze doors for the Florence baptistery before setting up on his own. Geometry and perspective became his ruling passion, taught in part by the mathematician Manetti. Vasari mocked the devotion as wasted time.

Yet his skill in foreshortening and proportion was remarkable, and his battle scenes and frescoes show a painter wrestling with depth on a flat wall. The entry weighs Vasari's gibe that he grew more needy than famous against the view that his experiments opened ground later painters used. It lists his chief works and their churches, offering a compact life of an artist remembered for his obsession as much as his pictures.
dick-prescott-s-second-year-at-west-poin:
Year two at West Point fills H. Irving Hancock's second Dick Prescott book, on finding the glory of the soldier's life. Twenty-four chapters open with the class president lecturing on hazing. Plebe Briggs learns a few things, and Greg debates between girls and mischief.

Dick stands under a fearful charge, in close arrest, and on trial by court-martial. Friends stand by, and a verdict and a hop follow. A new cadet corporal is named in orders in the sampled middle, with Mr Dodge taking the place of a busted Ryder. Prescott, it is said, would have had the post but for his name for dodging scrapes. Barracks fights, the riding drill, and baseball fill the rest of the year.
doe-osti-17171715-hawc-multi-messenger-a:
Joshua Litchfield, a SULI intern at Los Alamos mentored by Kelly Malone, built an alert system linking the HAWC gamma ray observatory with other detectors, in a report dated August 2026. Multi messenger astrophysics gains when one observatory's event is checked against another's in near real time. HAWC watches the sky for very high energy gamma rays from a mountain site.

Methods define a HAWC alert metric, then run a coincident event search with the IceCube neutrino observatory, looking for events that line up in time and direction. A likelihood study of the source LHAASO J2108+5157 tests the machinery on a known object. The system aims to flag joint events fast enough for follow up telescopes to catch fading sources.
doe-osti-2572976-bringing-inorganic-carb:
DOE Basic Energy Sciences final report DE-SC0018020, by Hannah S. Shafaat of Ohio State University and dated July 24, 2025, closes a project that ran from September 2017 to August 2023. Nature's CODH/ACS enzyme pair turns carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide and then into acetyl-CoA, a basic fuel of life. The chemistry is industrially tempting, but the enzymes are huge, fragile, and oxygen-sensitive, so their mechanisms stay murky.

Shafaat's group built small, sturdy stand-ins instead. Two small proteins, ferredoxin and azurin, were reworked to host versions of the enzyme active sites, including the unusual four-iron, four-sulfur, nickel cluster. One line of work aimed at an artificial carbon monoxide dehydrogenase in a semisynthetic construct. The other probed the synthase side. Studying the mimics was meant to reveal metal oxidation states, binding sites, and intermediate structures that the native system hides.
doe-osti-2575368-em-shaping-symmetry-and:
Final technical report DE-SC0022229, led by Gregory M. Grason of UMass Amherst with E. Bryan Coughlin and Edwin L. Thomas of Texas A&M, covers September 2021 to February 2025. Block copolymers self-assemble into triply-periodic networks, sponge-like nanostructures prized for photonics, supercapacitors, and filtration membranes. Almost all work had stuck at one symmetry, the cubic double gyroid, because nobody could predict how chain packing shapes the rest.

The project established a medial packing paradigm for these assemblies. Its measure, medial thickness, reads how far each polymer block stretches from the dividing surface into the domain's middle, a direct gauge of packing frustration. Slice-and-view electron microscopy rebuilt real domains in three dimensions so the measure could be checked against experiment. Field theory calculations confirmed that chains tend to follow the medial map. Twelve papers and two dissertations came out of the award.
doe-osti-2585494-water-cooled-helmholtz-:
Gabriel Wiser's report, SAND2025-09674R, presents the design of a water-cooled Helmholtz coil for ultra-low magnetic field testing. Precise work with very small fields suffers when stray fields and trapped flux in superconducting magnets shift the field a test object actually feels. The coil was designed to wrap around a helium-3 cryogenic fridge with a 17.825-inch outer diameter, both to zero out stray fields and to sharpen field sweeps.

Wiser supports the design with finite volume modeling and finite element analysis. The models show the coil can run at 20 amperes indefinitely, producing a field of 65 millitesla. At that load the surface facing the fridge stays below 50 degrees Celsius. The report also does the practical math of ownership: the full parts list comes to 4,882.76 dollars.
doe-osti-2588880-structural-uncertainty-:
Stefan Domino of Sandia National Laboratories wrote this report, SAND2025-11249, printed September 2025, on structural uncertainty in large eddy simulation. The question is not whether a turbulence model is wrong, all subgrid models are approximations, but how much the choice among respectable models moves the answer. Two canonical flows serve as the test beds: plane channel flow and the periodic hill.

Three subgrid models are compared in wall-resolved, low-Mach simulations: WALE, a standard k-equation model, and the Inagaki k-equation variant. Implementation details come first, then each flow is computed with each model. One clear finding concerns near-wall behavior. The static coefficient k-equation model shows non-standard asymptotic behavior near the wall, a first-order dependence on wall distance where theory expects otherwise. The low-Reynolds corrected Inagaki form behaves differently. Results like these show users which parts of a prediction are model choice, not physics.
doe-osti-2589495-methodology-for-determi:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-2800-96453 closes cooperative project CRD-21-21474 on lab methods for corn ethanol plants. Technical contacts Katie Michel and Justin Sluiter led work to measure the fiber part of corn kernels more completely. Plants earn credit under the Renewable Fuel Standard for the share of kernel fiber converted to fuel, so the measurement matters.

The method targets total cellulosic glucan, counting both cellulose and beta-glucans, plus hemicellulose, the other main fiber sugars. One task checked how much glucan is lost when samples pass through a cold caustic extraction step. Nuclear magnetic resonance runs on standard reference biomass confirmed starch signals that can confuse results. The outcome is one shared procedure the dry-grind ethanol industry can apply the same way at every plant.
doe-osti-3011000-preliminary-assessment-:
Low temperature chlorination of aluminium clad used nuclear fuel is assessed in SRNL-STI-2025-00645 by Vinh Nguyen and Thomas Shehee of Savannah River National Laboratory. Recent work with disulfur dichloride and thionyl chloride is summarised as groundwork for separating uranium from cladding and alloying elements. The assessment identifies two development needs, reaction kinetics and reagent quality.

A Uruguay fuel plate held at the laboratory, a U-Alx fuel meat with low enriched uranium and about 0.08 percent burnup, is analysed as a candidate for bench scale chlorination tests. Proposed next steps cover kinetic studies, reagent quality checks, and machining the plate to a suitable size before testing.
doe-osti-3011944-laboratory-investigatio:
Aerosol cloud interactions under entrainment are measured in a cloud chamber for the final report on award DE-SC0022128. Will Cantrell and Raymond Shaw of Michigan Tech led the work, with Fan Yang of Brookhaven National Laboratory. The Pi Chamber experiments are the first lab entrainment studies since Latham and Reed in 1977. Large eddy runs with the System for Atmospheric Modeling round out the measurements.

Droplet size response to mixing proved locally inhomogeneous yet globally homogeneous. The system rests in multiple equilibrium states, which explains the two readings. Simulations showed inhomogeneous marks for single mixing events but homogeneous pattern across an ensemble. Polluted clouds showed stronger inhomogeneous mixing in the model.
doe-osti-3015674-fundamentals-of-solar-p:
Why solar mounting bolts work loose is explained in a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report dated January 2026, by Jon Ness of Matrix Engineering Consultants and Gerald Robinson. Loose joints let modules shift, wear, and fail, and the report splits loosening into two families: rotation under vibration, and relaxation, where preload fades without the nut turning.

Relaxation mechanisms get the deep treatment: yielding of joint parts, fretting wear, surface embedment, and differential thermal expansion. Fixes follow the physics, including longer bolt grip lengths, Belleville springs, fewer joint interfaces, and washers sized to spread bearing stress. Retightening works but is often impractical across a solar field, which pushes design toward joints that hold preload from the start. A SETO failure survey grounds the mechanisms in field reports.
doe-osti-3023375-energy-cost-estimate-to:
Andrew Speake and Noel Merket of the National Laboratory of the Rockies document the Energy Cost Estimate Tool, version 2.0, in report NLR/TP-5500-95621, dated March 2026. The tool predicts home energy use and cost, and this volume explains the method behind it plus how to use it. Predictions lean on modeled building data rather than meter readings from each house.

Models were trained and checked with cross-validation, so test buildings were never seen during training. Median predictions are expected to be the most accurate and can be compared directly against the test dataset, unlike the other quartile regression models.
